areas.name: Accidental errors (people)
areas.rationale: Frequent slips, mostly small; occasional very large (fat-finger).
areas.good: Safe workplace; near misses and slips are reported and learned from; checks are built into routine work so simple errors are caught.
areas.loss: Keying, payment or instruction errors (wrong amount, account, security or recipient) cause direct losses, client compensation and data breaches.
areas.perf: Rework, correction effort and client apologies consume time; double-checking everything slows throughput.

areas.name: Training & competency
areas.rationale: Errors and unsuitable advice; strong driver of quality and productivity.
areas.good: Staff have the skills their roles need; training is planned and prioritised; skills are mapped to role requirements.
areas.loss: Staff who do not understand products, rules or systems give unsuitable advice, mis-execute, or miss red flags.
areas.perf: Slower work, more escalations and supervision, lower client service quality and weaker innovation.

areas.name: Resourcing & key people
areas.rationale: Skipped controls and key-person risk; burnout and attrition.
areas.good: Workloads are sustainable; critical tasks have trained cover; succession exists for key people.
areas.loss: Stretched teams skip or shorten checks, build backlogs (e.g., KYC reviews) and depend on single individuals.
areas.perf: Burnout, attrition and hiring costs; firefighting crowds out improvement and growth work.

areas.name: Roles & responsibilities
areas.rationale: Gaps between teams; duplicated effort.
areas.good: Clear, documented roles; individual ownership of processes and controls; no gaps or overlaps between teams.
areas.loss: Work and controls fall between people or teams; conflicting roles remove independent checks.
areas.perf: Duplicated effort, slow decisions and friction between teams.

areas.name: Communication
areas.rationale: Hand-off errors, usually moderate; efficiency drag.
areas.good: Timely, accurate information flows between teams and to leadership; a single source of truth; leadership hears the truth first-hand.
areas.loss: Information arrives late, incomplete or distorted; warnings are not escalated.
areas.perf: Rework, delays and decisions taken on stale or wrong information.

areas.name: Culture & speak-up
areas.rationale: Behind the largest conduct failures; drives engagement and retention.
areas.good: Shared vision; staff feel valued and safe to speak up; accountability and fair reward; continuous improvement encouraged.
areas.loss: Incentives and norms that tolerate rule-bending or silence lead to systemic misconduct and late discovery of problems.
areas.perf: Disengagement, turnover, silence about problems and lost ideas; culture is a major driver of productivity.

areas.name: Internal misconduct
areas.rationale: Rare but potentially severe (fraud, rogue trading).
areas.good: High integrity; ethical breaches have consequences regardless of seniority; trust backed by effective compliance oversight.
areas.loss: Deliberate wrongdoing by staff: fraud, unauthorised trading, theft of client funds or data.
areas.perf: Erosion of trust; heavy controls and investigations divert resources.

areas.name: Process & product design
areas.rationale: Repeated errors and mass client harm; cost-to-serve.
areas.good: Processes are defined, documented, efficient and have preventive controls built in.
areas.loss: Processes or products designed without adequate controls or suitability lead to repeated errors or mass mis-selling.
areas.perf: Unnecessary steps, approvals and hand-offs raise cost-to-serve and slow client service.

areas.name: Process execution
areas.rationale: Most frequent processing losses; workarounds and rework.
areas.good: Processes are followed consistently; non-adherence is identified; errors are caught before reaching clients or regulators.
areas.loss: Processes not followed or controls not operating: missed checks, unreconciled breaks, KYC not done.
areas.perf: Workarounds, rework and inconsistent output; quality depends on who does the work.

areas.name: Change & projects
areas.rationale: Outages and errors from change; delivery capacity limits growth.
areas.good: Change is planned, resourced, tested and communicated; benefits are tracked and realised.
areas.loss: Poorly planned or tested change introduces errors, outages and data problems.
areas.perf: Benefits not realised, change fatigue, delayed strategy.

areas.name: Governance & oversight
areas.rationale: Root cause in most major failures; decision quality.
areas.good: Management understand how the business works; clear accountability and decision-making; policies understood; outsourced providers actively overseen.
areas.loss: Leadership lacks information, challenge or accountability, so risks accumulate unseen (incl. outsourced providers).
areas.perf: Slow or poor decisions; strategy not executed; resources misallocated.

areas.name: Systems functionality & capacity
areas.rationale: Workarounds and confusing systems cause errors; major productivity driver.
areas.good: Systems support end-to-end processes without manual gaps; data and reports are trusted.
areas.loss: Systems that do not fit processes force manual workarounds, re-keying and confusing interfaces that cause errors.
areas.perf: Manual effort, slow processing, poor data for decisions and limits on scale.

areas.name: Availability & maintenance
areas.rationale: Outages and unsupported software / key-person spreadsheets.
areas.good: Software and devices are current and supported; critical spreadsheets/tools are controlled.
areas.loss: Unpatched or unsupported software is exploited or fails; uncontrolled spreadsheets produce errors.
areas.perf: Fragile, slow tools; dependence on individuals; costly emergency fixes.

areas.name: Systems change delivery
areas.rationale: Escaped defects and faulty releases; occasionally severe.
areas.good: The business specifies and tests changes; systems work as expected at go-live.
areas.loss: Changes or models not properly tested produce wrong results in live use.
areas.perf: Defects cost more to fix later; users lose confidence in systems.

areas.name: Cyber security & access
areas.rationale: Cyber and email-enabled fraud are among the most frequent losses for small firms.
areas.good: Access and configuration are controlled; least-privilege access; prompt removal on moves and leavers.
areas.loss: Wrong settings or excessive access expose data or allow wrong processing (e.g., wrong fee tables).
areas.perf: Access requests and fixes consume IT and user time.

areas.name: Data & records
areas.rationale: Record-keeping failures; time lost finding information.
areas.good: Staff know what to keep, where and for how long; records are findable; destruction is controlled.
areas.loss: Records lost, kept too long, disposed of insecurely or not producible for regulators.
areas.perf: Time wasted searching for information; duplicated documents and versions.

areas.name: Technology planning
areas.rationale: Slow-burn cause of legacy and change problems; limits growth.
areas.good: IT plans follow business strategy; sufficient investment and expertise; lock-in managed.
areas.loss: Under-investment, lock-in and poor IT strategy leave the firm with fragile, outdated technology.
areas.perf: Technology fails to support growth; high running costs; competitors move faster.

areas.name: External fraud
areas.rationale: Impersonation, payment and counterparty fraud are frequent and costly.
areas.good: Instructions and requests are independently verified; counterparties are subject to due diligence; robust anti-fraud checks.
areas.loss: Clients, suppliers or counterparties commit fraud (fake instructions, forged documents, impersonation).
areas.perf: Extra verification friction; limited performance impact.

areas.name: Physical & environmental events
areas.rationale: Rare for most office-based firms; exposure depends on locations.
areas.good: Business continuity plans are clear, known and tested; critical work can continue remotely.
areas.loss: Pandemics, floods or earthquakes disrupt premises, people and providers.
areas.perf: Lost productivity during disruption; costs of relocation.

areas.name: Geopolitical & regulatory change
areas.rationale: Sanctions and regulatory change bring fines, remediation and exits.
areas.good: The firm considers how geopolitical or economic shocks affect clients and operations.
areas.loss: Sanctions, conflict or instability in client, counterparty or provider jurisdictions freeze assets or force rapid exits.
areas.perf: Business lost in affected markets; management time absorbed.

statements.text: My workplace is physically safe, and accidents or near misses are reported and learned from.
Simple slips (e.g., wrong figure, wrong recipient) are rare because checks are built into how we work.
In the last 3 months, how often did a mistake by you or your team reach a client, counterparty or other external party?
I have the knowledge and skills I need to do my job well, including the rules that apply to it.
In the last 12 months I received training or development that genuinely improved how I do my job.
How often are you asked to do tasks you do not feel competent to do, without support?
I can complete my work to the required standard within my normal working hours.
If I were unexpectedly absent for two weeks, someone else could do my critical tasks without serious problems.
In the last month, how often were checks or controls skipped or shortened because there was not enough time?
I am clear what I am personally responsible for, including any checks or controls I own.
It is clear which team is responsible for each activity, so work does not fall between teams or get duplicated.
How often does work stall or get missed because nobody is sure who should do it?
Information I need from other teams reaches me on time, complete and accurate.
Senior management have an accurate picture of what really happens day to day in my area.
In the last 3 months, how often did you act on information that later turned out to be out of date or wrong?
I could raise a concern about a mistake or wrongdoing without fear of negative consequences.
People here are motivated, feel valued and would recommend the firm as a place to work.
In the last 6 months, I stayed silent about a problem because raising it seemed pointless or risky.
In the last 6 months I have felt pressure to bend rules or procedures to get things done.
Unethical behaviour has real consequences here, regardless of seniority or performance.
If I reported misconduct by a senior or high-performing colleague, I am confident it would be investigated fairly.
The processes I follow are documented, up to date and easy to find.
Our processes are efficient, without unnecessary steps, approvals or duplication.
Key processes have controls built in that prevent errors, rather than relying on catching them afterwards.
When a process involves several teams, the hand-off points (who passes what, when, and how it is checked) are clearly defined.
I often have to use manual workarounds (spreadsheets, emails, re-keying) because the standard process or system does not work.
Processes are followed consistently, whoever is doing the work.
Errors in my area are caught before they reach clients, counterparties or regulators.
In the last 3 months, how often did you see a required check signed off without being properly done?
Changes to processes or systems that affect me are planned, tested and explained before they go live.
Recent changes in my area have delivered the benefits that were promised.
The firm has the capacity and skills to deliver change alongside day-to-day work.
In the last 12 months, a change in my area caused errors, outages or client issues after it went live.
When something goes wrong, it is clear who is accountable for fixing it, and it gets fixed.
Decisions that affect my work are made in good time, based on facts, and explained clearly.
Our key outsourced providers (e.g., fund administrator, IT provider) are actively overseen, with clear owners and escalation when service falls short.
The systems I use support my work well, without needing workarounds.
I trust the data and reports our systems produce.
Our systems stay fast and responsive at busy times (e.g., month-end, market events).
How often do you find that two systems or reports show different figures for the same thing?
I rely on spreadsheets or self-built tools that only a few people understand for important calculations or reports.
The systems I need are available whenever I need them.
Users are involved in specifying and testing new or changed systems before they go live.
New systems or system changes work as expected when they go live.
I am told in advance about system changes and know how to get help if something goes wrong afterwards.
Spreadsheets and models used for important outputs are checked by someone other than their author before first use.
I have access to systems or data that I do not need for my current role.
In my team, clients or colleagues use personal messaging apps or personal email (e.g., WhatsApp, Gmail) to discuss work matters.
Shared logins or passwords are used for some systems I work with.
I know where information must be stored, how long it must be kept and how it must be disposed of.
I can quickly find the information and records I need.
Client and business records are kept in approved, backed-up locations rather than personal drives, email folders or desktops.
The tools and systems I use have kept pace with how the business has grown.
When I need help to use a system properly, I can quickly get it from someone who knows it well.
Technology decisions involve the people who will use the systems.
Scenario: an email that appears to come from a long-standing client asks you to send funds urgently to a new bank account. What do you do?
I know what to do, and could keep doing my critical work, if our office or key systems became unavailable.
I have taken part in a business continuity test or exercise in the last 12 months.
We hear about regulatory changes early and implement them on time without disrupting the business.
I am told about regulatory changes that affect my work before they take effect, with practical guidance on what to do differently.

bands.label: Weak
bands.meaning: Good practice is largely absent; losses and under-performance likely.

bands.label: Developing
bands.meaning: Good practice is patchy or informal.

bands.label: Established
bands.meaning: Good practice is in place most of the time - the baseline for a well-run small firm.

bands.label: Strong
bands.meaning: Good practice is consistent and embedded.

bands.label: Leading
bands.meaning: Good practice is how the firm works; a source of advantage.

archetypes.name: Fragile
archetypes.description: Exposed to loss and under-performing. Fix the basics first.

archetypes.name: Exposed
archetypes.description: Getting by, but controls are thin. A single event could hurt.

archetypes.name: High-wire
archetypes.description: Performing well while taking unmanaged risk; growth may be outrunning control.

archetypes.name: Stalled
archetypes.description: Adequately controlled, but processes and capacity hold performance back.

archetypes.name: Steady
archetypes.description: Middle of the pack. Targeted fixes will move both dials.

archetypes.name: Accelerating
archetypes.description: Strong performer; strengthen controls to protect the gains.

archetypes.name: Fortress
archetypes.description: Well controlled but inefficient; control may be stifling performance.

archetypes.name: Guarded
archetypes.description: Well protected, with performance still to unlock.

archetypes.name: Resilient performer
archetypes.description: Strong on both. Sustain, and use as a benchmark.
